title: Why Are Some Leaders Praise Stingy?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece explains why high-standards leaders tend to withhold praise and argues that they should stop. It says that a leader who sees every process as improvable focuses on results and so gives less recognition than people want, leaving a team working harder and disappointed. It adds a psychological observation that leaders tend to give the amount of praise they themselves need, so leaders who need little struggle to understand why others crave it. The corrective is a reframe of praise as a tool: specific, timely praise marks actions worth repeating and strengthens bonds. The closing claim is that the more leaders praise, the more people produce praiseworthy outcomes.
points: High expectations produce praise stinginess because a leader focused on results and continuous improvement rarely sees work as finished.
Leaders tend to give the amount of praise they personally need, so praise-indifferent leaders underestimate how much others want.
Praise is a steering tool: specific and timely recognition tells people which behaviors to replicate.
Withholding praise is a leadership failure of role awareness, since leaders prime and reinforce the behaviors they want to see.
Praise also strengthens leader-team bonds, so even results-driven leaders have a performance reason to use it.
quotes: Great leaders are notorious for their demanding expectations and high standards. They expect a lot from themselves and others and seek excellence in every step along the way to superior outcomes.

Leaders with high expectations and standards generally don’t offer the amount of praise those around them desire. Their focus on results and continuous improvement inhibits their willingness to offer praise.

Those around them work ever harder to earn their leader’s recognition, but often walk away disappointed. Leaders with high expectations hold praise like diamonds in a vault. They don’t offer those diamonds freely or to just anyone.

Interestingly, leaders are more likely to offer the amount of praise they themselves need. Those leaders who need or covet praise are generally more likely to offer it, while those who define success in more objective terms generally deprive others of the positive reinforcement they crave.

Good leaders recognize that praise focuses attention on actions worth repeating. The more specific and timely it is, the more it encourages people to replicate their actions. Leaders who don’t praise fail to realize their role in priming and reinforcing the behaviors they want to see from others.

Praise not only strengthens the bonds between leaders and team members, but it also shows people what is important to replicate. Even the most results-driven leaders can recognize the value of reiterating critical actions.
